titles.Retinal neurons & glia: Connecting nerve cells and Müller glia

Choroid & sclera.description: The sclera is the tough white outer wall of the eyeball, made of dense collagen that continues with the optic nerve sheath behind and the cornea in front. Behind the retina, the choroid is a pigmented, highly vascular layer that supplies the outer retina through its inner capillary bed, the choriocapillaris, which sits against Bruch membrane.
clinical: Uveal melanoma
The choroid is the most common site of uveal melanoma, the most common primary cancer inside the eye in adults. The tumour grows from melanocytes in this pigmented layer.
Wet age-related macular degeneration
New vessels grow from the choriocapillaris through a break in Bruch membrane and leak fluid and blood beneath the macula. Anti-VEGF injections are the standard treatment.

Outer retina.description: The outer retina is the light-sensing region. The retinal pigment epithelium absorbs stray light and recycles the pigment that photoreceptors use, while rods and cones have outer segments packed with light-sensitive pigment. Rods work in dim light, and cones give colour vision and sharp detail in bright light.
clinical: Retinitis pigmentosa
In this inherited condition, rods die first, causing night blindness and loss of peripheral vision, and cones are lost later.
Age-related macular degeneration

With ageing, waste (lipofuscin) builds up in the pigment epithelium and drusen form beneath it. In dry AMD, the pigment layer and overlying photoreceptors of the macula slowly waste away, causing central vision loss.

Neural retina layers.description: The neural retina is built from stacked layers of nerve cell bodies, separated by layers where synapses form. Signals pass from photoreceptors through bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons form the nerve fibre layer and leave the eye as the optic nerve.
clinical: Glaucoma
Glaucoma causes progressive loss of retinal ganglion cells and thinning of the nerve fibre layer, producing characteristic blind spots in the visual field.
Diabetic macular oedema
Leaking capillaries in diabetes cause fluid to collect in the macula, mainly in the inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers, which blurs central vision.
Congenital night blindness
Some inherited forms of congenital night blindness are caused by GRM6 mutations, which disable the mGluR6 receptor that ON bipolar cells need to receive rod and cone signals.

Retinal vessels.description: The inner retina has its own blood supply from the central retinal artery, whose branches run in the nerve fibre layer and are end arteries, so each branch supplies its own territory. The superficial and deep capillary beds feed the inner layers, while the outer retina depends on the choroid instead.
clinical: Central retinal artery occlusion
Retinal arteries are end arteries with no backup supply, so a blocked central retinal artery causes sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye.
Diabetic retinopathy
High blood sugar damages the pericytes that support retinal capillaries, causing microaneurysms, leakage and capillary dropout in the superficial and deep plexuses.

Inner limiting membrane & vitreous.description: The inner limiting membrane is the thin basement membrane made by the end-feet of Müller cells, forming the boundary between the retina and the vitreous. The vitreous body is a clear gel of collagen fibrils and hyaluronan that fills the eye in front of the retina and is attached most firmly at the optic disc, the macula and the vitreous base.
clinical: Posterior vitreous detachment
With age the vitreous gel can pull away from the retina, causing flashes and floaters. Sometimes the pull tears the retina, which can lead to retinal detachment.
Macular hole and epiretinal membrane surgery
Eye surgeons peel the inner limiting membrane during vitrectomy to close macular holes and remove scar membranes that pull on the macula.

parts.description: The sclera is the tough, opaque white outer wall of the eyeball, forming most of its outer coat, with the transparent cornea at the front. Its dense irregular collagen fibres protect the eye and maintain its shape, and the extraocular muscles attach to its outer surface. Behind the eye it is continuous with the dural sheath of the optic nerve, and in a section it appears as a dense, pink fibrous layer with few cells.

The choroid stroma is the loose connective tissue core of the choroid, the dark, vascular coat lying between the sclera and the retina. It contains collagen fibres, fibroblasts, pigment-producing melanocytes and a dense network of blood vessels, with the largest vessels in its outer layers. In a section it appears as a pale, loosely arranged matrix full of vessels and brown-pigmented cells, and it lies just outside the choriocapillaris, the capillary layer that feeds the outer retina.

Choroidal veins (Haller layer) form the outermost part of the choroid, lying just inside the sclera. They are mostly large, thin-walled veins that collect blood from the choroid and drain it out of the eye through the vortex veins, which pierce the sclera. In a section they appear as wide, thin-walled vessels on the scleral side of the choroid, with the smaller arteries of the Sattler layer lying on their inner side.

Choroidal arteries (Sattler layer) are medium-sized arteries forming the middle layer of the choroid, between the outer Haller layer of veins and the inner choriocapillaris. They arise from the short posterior ciliary arteries, and their small branches supply the choriocapillaris. In a section, they appear as muscular-walled arterial profiles lying between the large veins outside and the fine capillary network inside.

Choroidal melanocytes are pigment-producing cells scattered through the choroid stroma, with branching processes that spread among the blood vessels. They make melanin, which gives the choroid its dark colour and absorbs stray light so that it does not scatter inside the eye. In a section they appear as star-shaped cells packed with brown granules, and choroidal melanoma, the most common primary intraocular malignant tumour in adults, arises from them.

The choriocapillaris is the innermost layer of the choroid, a dense, flat network of fenestrated capillaries lying directly beneath Bruch membrane. It supplies the outer retina, including the photoreceptors and the retinal pigment epithelium, which have no blood vessels of their own. Fenestrated means the capillary walls have pores that allow rapid exchange of oxygen and nutrients. In a section it appears as a single layer of closely packed, thin-walled capillaries.

Bruch membrane is the thin, five-layered basement membrane lying between the retinal pigment epithelium and the choriocapillaris. It acts as a selective filter that controls the passage of nutrients and waste between the retina and the choroid. In a section it appears as a fine, homogeneous line, and it thickens with age. Drusen, small deposits that collect between the pigment epithelium and this membrane, are an early sign of age-related macular degeneration.

The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is a single layer of pigmented cells lying between the photoreceptors and Bruch membrane, and it is essential for photoreceptor survival. Its melanin absorbs stray light, it recycles the visual pigment that photoreceptors use, and it engulfs the worn tips of their outer segments every day. In a section it appears as a single layer of dark, cuboidal cells with brown granules, with fine microvilli reaching between the outer segments.

Rod outer segments are the long, slender light-sensing tips of rod photoreceptors, lying beyond the outer limiting membrane against the retinal pigment epithelium. Each contains a stack of membranous discs packed with the light-sensitive pigment rhodopsin, and new discs are added continually at the base. Rods respond to dim light and are used for night vision. In a section they form a thin, pale, layered band next to the microvilli of the retinal pigment epithelium.

Rod inner segments are the part of each rod photoreceptor that joins its outer segment to its cell body. Their outer region, the ellipsoid, is packed with mitochondria that supply the energy needed to run the cell's ion pumps. They lie on the retinal pigment epithelium side of the outer limiting membrane, and in a section they form a dense, granular band.

Cones are the cone-shaped photoreceptors responsible for colour vision and sharp central vision. They are densest in the fovea, the cone-rich centre of the macula, and their short, tapered outer segments contain pigments sensitive to red, green or blue light. Cones work best in bright light, and their nuclei are larger and paler than those of rods, which helps to tell the two apart in a section.

The outer limiting membrane is not a true membrane but a row of junctions between Müller glia (the retina's support cells) and the photoreceptors, lying at the boundary between the photoreceptor inner segments and the outer nuclear layer. These junctions anchor the photoreceptor cells and help to hold the outer retina in its layered arrangement. In a section it appears as a thin, dark line, and it is a useful landmark for locating the photoreceptor layers.

The outer nuclear layer is the band of photoreceptor cell bodies, containing the nuclei of rods and cones, which lies between the outer limiting membrane and the outer plexiform layer. Rod nuclei are small, dark and very densely packed, whereas cone nuclei are larger and paler. Each photoreceptor sends its axon inwards to synapse in the outer plexiform layer, where its signal is passed on.

The outer plexiform layer is the synaptic zone between the outer and inner nuclear layers, where photoreceptor terminals contact the dendrites of horizontal cells and bipolar cells. Rod spherules and cone pedicles, the swollen synaptic endings of the photoreceptors, are seen here. In a section it appears as a pale, fibrous band with few nuclei, which makes it easy to recognise between the two nuclear layers.

The inner nuclear layer contains the cell bodies of bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells and Müller glia (the retina's support cells), and lies between the outer and inner plexiform layers. The neurons here relay and modify signals passing from the photoreceptors towards the ganglion cells. In a section it is a band of dark, round nuclei sitting between two pale, fibrous synaptic layers.

Horizontal cells are interneurons whose cell bodies lie at the outer edge of the inner nuclear layer, and whose wide, flat dendritic processes spread through the outer plexiform layer. They receive input from photoreceptors and feed signals back onto photoreceptor terminals, creating the centre-surround organisation (lateral inhibition) of receptive fields that sharpens contrast. In a section they appear as a sparse set of nuclei at the outer edge of the inner nuclear layer.

Bipolar cells are the relay neurons that carry signals from photoreceptors to ganglion cells, with dendrites in the outer plexiform layer and axons ending in the inner plexiform layer. Their cell bodies lie in the inner nuclear layer. ON bipolar cells, which depolarise in light, end in the inner half of the inner plexiform layer, while OFF bipolar cells, which hyperpolarise in light, end in the outer half. They carry graded potentials rather than spikes, and rod bipolar cells are all of the ON type.

Amacrine cells are interneurons whose cell bodies lie at the inner edge of the inner nuclear layer, and whose processes spread in the inner plexiform layer; they have no conventional axon. There are many types, including AII cells that relay rod signals into cone pathways, starburst cells that detect the direction of motion using acetylcholine and GABA as neurotransmitters, and dopaminergic cells that help the retina adapt to bright light. In a section they are recognised by their position at the inner edge of the inner nuclear layer.

The inner plexiform layer is the synaptic zone between the inner nuclear layer and the ganglion cell layer, where bipolar cell axons contact amacrine cell processes and ganglion cell dendrites. It is divided into sublayers, with ON pathways synapsing in its inner half and OFF pathways in its outer half. In a section it appears as a pale, fibrous band with few nuclei, lying between the two cell-body layers.

The ganglion cell layer contains the cell bodies of retinal ganglion cells, the output neurons of the retina whose axons form the nerve fibre layer and leave the eye as the optic nerve. It lies between the inner plexiform layer and the nerve fibre layer. In a section, ganglion cells are relatively large neurons with large, pale nuclei and prominent nucleoli, and some displaced amacrine cells are scattered among them.

The nerve fibre layer is the innermost layer of the neural retina, made of the unmyelinated axons of retinal ganglion cells running towards the optic disc. It lies directly beneath the inner limiting membrane, next to the vitreous, and carries the branches of the retinal arteries and veins. On ophthalmoscopy it appears as fine streaks radiating from the optic disc, and loss of its fibres is an early feature of glaucoma.

Retinal arterioles are the small arteries that branch from the central retinal artery and run across the inner retina, mainly in the nerve fibre and ganglion cell layers. They have thick muscular walls that regulate blood flow, and they are end arteries, so each branch supplies its own territory with little overlap. A blocked branch therefore causes a wedge-shaped area of visual loss. On ophthalmoscopy they look brighter red and narrower than the accompanying veins.

Retinal venules are the small veins that collect blood from the capillary networks of the inner retina and join to form the central retinal vein, which leaves the eye through the optic nerve. They run alongside the arterioles in the nerve fibre layer and have thinner walls than the arterioles. On ophthalmoscopy they look darker and wider than the arterioles, which is the usual way to tell them apart.

The superficial capillary plexus is the network of capillaries lying in the nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell layer, fed by branches of the retinal arterioles. It nourishes the nerve fibre layer, the ganglion cell layer and the inner part of the inner plexiform layer. In a section it appears as thin-walled capillary profiles scattered among the ganglion cells and their axons.

The deep capillary plexus is a network of capillaries lying in the outer part of the inner nuclear layer, close to the outer plexiform layer. It is fed by penetrating branches from the superficial plexus and supplies the inner nuclear layer and the outer plexiform layer. It is absent from the foveal centre, which is why the fovea depends on the choroid for its oxygen.

Müller glia (Müller cells) are the main glial cells of the retina, radial cells that span the full thickness of the neural retina, from microvilli reaching past the outer limiting membrane to end-feet at the inner limiting membrane. Their nuclei lie in the inner nuclear layer, and their conical end-feet form the inner limiting membrane. They buffer potassium, recycle glutamate through the enzyme glutamine synthetase, store glycogen and may guide light to the photoreceptors.

The inner limiting membrane is a thin basement membrane forming the innermost surface of the retina, where it separates the nerve fibre layer from the vitreous body. It is made mainly by the conical end-feet of Müller glia (the retina's support cells), and the vitreous gel rests against its surface. In a section it appears as a fine, continuous line at the surface of the retina, and surgeons peel it away in some operations for macular holes.

The vitreous body is the transparent, gel-like substance that fills the large cavity of the eye behind the lens and lies in front of the retina. It is almost entirely water, held in a meshwork of fine collagen fibrils and hyaluronan, and it helps keep the retina pressed against the choroid. It is attached most firmly to the optic disc, the macula and the vitreous base at the ora serrata, the anterior edge of the retina.
